source_read: PMC HTML full text, PMC3380537 (author manuscript of J Abnorm Psychol 2012;121(2):511-523), read in full in the reader's own browser tab: all sections, footnotes, Tables 1-3 (HTML tables). Figure 2 (rates among people at risk, by age) was not viewable (screenshot blank); no value used by the claim depends on it, because the two persistence rates the claim uses are printed in the Discussion text.

claims.overstatement: None for the part from this source: the claim says 'no longer met the full criteria', not 'recovered' or 'remitted', and says treatment is not reported. Points of precision: (1) 1,172 is not printed in the paper; it is the editors' sum of two Table 2 columns (Persistence N=422 + past-year dependence at Wave 1 without dependence at Wave 2 N=750), so the 'editors' calculation from unweighted counts' label should cover the 1,172 and the 36% as well as the 64%. (2) The unweighted 36%/64% come from a sample that oversampled young adults aged 18-24 and Black and Hispanic people, so they are not population estimates; the 32.4% and 44.5% are the paper's own rates from its weighted (SUDAAN) analysis. (3) The age bands are approximate ages at the second interview (age at Wave 1 plus three years), and the interval between interviews varied between people. (4) 'Met them again in the year before the second' is correct as worded; the paper's persistence group includes people whose dependence was episodic and who had a remission between the interviews that did not reach into the year before Wave 2. (5) 'No longer met the full criteria' is one past-year window about three years later, not sustained remission.
claims.note: All numbers from this source recomputed: 422 + 750 = 1,172 (all six Table 2 groups sum exactly to the 34,653 re-interviewed, so 1,172 is every re-interviewed person with past-year dependence at Wave 1); 422/1,172 = 36.0%; 750/1,172 = 64.0%. 32.4% (ages 21-23) and 44.5% (ages 43-52) as printed. Treatment: the full text was searched; treatment is not mentioned anywhere in the article (the only string match is an author name in the references), which confirms the claim's 'treatment between the interviews is not reported'. Optional addition not in the claim: among people with past but not past-year dependence at Wave 1 (already in remission for at least a year), 244 of 2,785 (8.8%, editors' calculation, unweighted, Table 2) met the criteria again in the year before Wave 2. The analysis sample for Table 3 is smaller (993 with past-year dependence at baseline, 363 persistent, 36.6%) because of missing life-transition data; this agrees with the 36%. The paper's main finding is that the fall in dependence with age comes mostly from fewer new onsets and recurrences, while persistence is fairly stable across adulthood (rising slightly with age); this fits the claim's use.

anchors.extracted: NESARC, a survey funded by NIAAA and run by the US Census Bureau, representative of US civilians aged 18 and over; oversampled Black and Hispanic people and young adults aged 18-24; face-to-face interviews in 2001-2002 (43,093 respondents) and again in 2004-2005 (34,653 of the same respondents); data weighted to the US population; Wave 2 mean age 48.

anchors.locator: Method › Measures › Alcohol Dependence, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 2 (column headers)
anchors.extracted: Alcohol dependence by DSM-IV criteria (at least 3 of 7) assessed with the AUDADIS-IV, for the past 12 months and before the past 12 months. Persistence group: past-12-month dependence at Wave 1 and at Wave 2, n = 422. Table 2: past-12-month dependence at Wave 1 but none at Wave 2, N = 750. Editors' sum 1,172; 422/1,172 = 36.0% and 750/1,172 = 64.0% (unweighted, recomputed). Persistence is defined to include episodic dependence: a remission during the follow-up that did not extend to the year before Wave 2 still counts as persistence.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Rethinking the Dramatic Age-Gradient in the Prevalence Curve of Alcohol Disorders, 1st paragraph; Results, paragraph after Figure 1; Figure 2 caption
anchors.extracted: Persistence rates of dependence 32.4% at ages 21-23 and 44.5% at ages 43-52 (among people with past-year dependence at Wave 1); the authors call this difference a minor contributor to the age gradient and persistence relatively stable across the third decade. In logistic regressions adjusted for sex and race, persistence showed an increasing trend with age (Wald F = 2.28, 6 df, p = .047; not significant in the multiple-imputation analyses), while onset (Wald F = 44.22) and recurrence (Wald F = 6.64) fell significantly with age (both p < .0001). Age groups are based on age at Wave 1, so the ages shown approximate age at Wave 2.

anchors.locator: Results › Alternative Definitions of Persistence and Recurrence, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Persistence required meeting full criteria at Wave 2, so a person with one or two dependence symptoms at Wave 2 counted as not persistent. Reanalysed as dependence at Wave 1 plus at least one symptom at Wave 2, persistence rose in every age group (no figures given) with a similar age pattern; requiring continuous dependence across the interval instead showed no significant change with age.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Rethinking the Dramatic Age-Gradient in the Prevalence Curve of Alcohol Disorders, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: The authors' persistence (past-year dependence at Wave 2 among people with past-year dependence at Wave 1, a common 3-year window) disagrees with Grant's (1997) cross-sectional definition (past-year dependence among people with dependence before the past year); using Grant's definition on Wave 1 NESARC data they reproduced her age-related decrease (results not shown). They conclude that different definitions of persistence can give conflicting findings about age.

anchors.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Retention about 80%. Retained at Wave 2: 79.1% of people with current dependence at Wave 1 vs 81.2% of people with no diagnosis (not significantly different) and 85.6% of people with dependence only before the past year (significantly higher). Wave 2 weights adjusted for attrition; multiple imputation gave similar results. All data self-reported.

anchors.locator: Method › Measures › Alcohol Dependence, 2nd paragraph; Table 2 (Recurrence and 'Lifetime but no 12 MO AD W1' columns)
anchors.extracted: Not used by the claim. People with dependence before, but not in, the year before Wave 1: 244 met the criteria again in the year before Wave 2 (Recurrence group) and 2,541 did not; 244/2,785 = 8.8% (editors' calculation, unweighted).
